Choosing the school is the first half of MTL-101. The second half asks whether the kilometre
around that school is somewhere the family wants to live. This post runs the second half on
five francophone public elementary schools: the four CSSDM schools the project brief uses as
seed data, and one Outremont neighbourhood school under the CSS Marguerite-Bourgeoys as a
contrast. Every number comes from open data published by the Ville de Montréal, the Quebec
government or Statistics Canada, pulled and aggregated by the scripts in the repository.

The zone is a circle of one kilometre around the school building, roughly a twelve-minute walk.
That is a stand-in, not the real catchment: the Ministry's geospatial download contains school
service centre boundaries and school points but no per-school zone polygons, so the true zones
exist only in the service centres' finders and PDF maps. Everything with point, parcel or
dissemination-area granularity is aggregated into the circle. Dissemination areas count when
their centroid falls inside it.

::: {.callout-important}
## Not a ranking

The tables report each metric with its decile among the 229 francophone public elementary
schools on the island outside the West Island, marked [d1]{.decile-low} to [d3]{.decile-low}
for the lowest three tenths, [d4]{.decile-mid} to [d7]{.decile-mid} for the middle, and
[d8]{.decile-high} to [d10]{.decile-high} for the top three. A high decile means a high value,
nothing more: d10 on income and d10 on break-ins are both "top tenth". The post computes no
composite score, and the IMSE does not appear here on purpose. The IMSE is a socioeconomic
index of the pupils a school actually enrols, not an academic ranking, and it can diverge from
the census figures below, which describe the residents of the circle whether or not their
children attend the school.
:::

| Collisions routières | Ville de Montréal (SAAQ) | pedestrian and cyclist victims per collision | point | 2012 to 2021 |
| Imposition annuelle de taxes municipales | Ville de Montréal | every tax line on every account: assessed value, rate, amount | account | 2021 to 2026 |

| Localisation des établissements d'enseignement | MEQ, Données Québec | school points, codes, service centre | point | 2026 |

# How the numbers are made

Six commands take the portals' files to the tables below. The fetcher resolves download URLs
through the portals' CKAN APIs, so a re-published file keeps working; the two `prep` steps
collapse the heavy files once; `census_da` streams the 6.4 GB Quebec census file and keeps the
island's 3,228 dissemination areas.

```bash
uv run scripts/fetch_open_data.py --core taxes                                  # <1>
uv run scripts/prep_taxes.py                                                    # <2>
uv run scripts/prep_uev.py                                                      # <3>
uv run scripts/census_da.py                                                     # <4>
uv run scripts/zone_stats.py --all                                              # <5>
uv run scripts/zone_stats.py "Saint-Barthélemy" "La Vérendrye" "Charles-Lemoyne" \
    "Saint-Nom-de-Jésus" "Saint-Germain-d'Outremont"                            # <6>
```
1. downloads about 3.5 GB into `data/raw/` and writes a manifest with fetch dates; `taxes` is the 19 borough tax-bill files
2. one row per tax account: assessed value from the general-tax line, total bill, class (residential 5 dwellings or fewer, 6 or more, non-residential, vacant)
3. one point per assessment unit with dwelling count, year built and condo flag, from the 780 MB GeoJSON
4. the census variables per island dissemination area, cached as parquet
5. every island school, which is what the deciles are measured against
6. the five schools of this post, as a Markdown table

The tax file is the least familiar of the sources and the one that replaces the commercial
price and tax sites a parent would otherwise use. One residential account in 2026 is seven
lines, each with the same assessed value and its own rate:

```
CODE  DESCR_LONGUE                                        VAL_IMPOSABLE  TAUX_IMPOSI  MONTANT_DETAIL
B00   TAXE GÉNÉRALE : CAT. IMM. RÉSIDUELLE (5 LOG. OU -)      2500767.0  0.004631000        11581.05
Q00   TAXE ARTM : CATEGORIE IMM. RESIDUELLE                    2500767.0  0.000070000          175.05
Q00   DETTE ANC.VILLE : CATEGORIE IMM. RESIDUELLE              2500767.0  0.000052000          130.04
J00   TAXE SPÉCIALE EAU : CAT. IMM. RÉSIDUELLE                 2500767.0  0.000831000         2078.14
I00   TAXE SPÉCIALE VOIRIE : RÉSIDENTIEL                       2500767.0  0.000024000           60.02
E00   TAXE RELATIVE AUX SERVICES                               2500767.0  0.000431000         1077.83
P20   TAXE RELATIVE AUX INVESTISSEMENTS                        2500767.0  0.000298000          745.23
```

The sum of the last column is the bill. The last two lines are the borough's own taxes, which
is where borough rates differ; the first is the city-wide general tax. Joining the account to
its parcel on the assessment-unit id succeeds for 99.7% of accounts, and the parcel supplies
the dwelling count that separates a single-family house from a plex.

# The five zones

- **Saint-Barthélemy** (Villeray). IB primary years programme, selective admission. The school
  has two pavilions about 450 m apart; the circle is drawn around pavillon Sagard, where the
  Ministry places the school point.
- **La Vérendrye** (Tétreaultville, Mercier-Hochelaga-Maisonneuve). IB primary years programme
  with non-selective admission, lottery only if oversubscribed. Façade and masonry work was
  under way in autumn 2025 with pupils in place.[^lv]
- **Charles-Lemoyne** (Pointe-Saint-Charles, Le Sud-Ouest). Freinet alternative pedagogy with an
  environmental focus. Façade and window replacement was under way in autumn 2025 with pupils
  in place.[^cl]
- **Saint-Nom-de-Jésus** (Hochelaga-Maisonneuve). Freinet alternative pedagogy, admission by
  lottery split 60/40 between the catchment and the rest of the CSSDM. The school site was not
  reachable when this was written, so its renovation status is unverified.
- **Saint-Germain-d'Outremont** (Outremont, CSS Marguerite-Bourgeoys). A neighbourhood school,
  included as the contrast. A new Outremont primary school on the Campus MIL is due to open in
  autumn 2026 and will redraw the borough's zones.[^sgo]

[^lv]: [Info-travaux, août 2025](https://la-verendrye.cssdm.gouv.qc.ca/nouvelles/info-travaux-aout-2025/), École La Vérendrye.
[^cl]: [Info-travaux, août 2025](https://charles-lemoyne.cssdm.gouv.qc.ca/nouvelles/info-travaux-aout-2025/), École Charles-Lemoyne.
[^sgo]: [Une nouvelle école primaire à Outremont](https://journaloutremont.com/nouvelles/vie-scolaire/une-nouvelle-ecole-primaire-a-outremont), Journal d'Outremont.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reading the table

The two Hochelaga-Maisonneuve zones are not alike. Tétreaultville, around La Vérendrye, sits
near the island median on almost every line. Hochelaga proper, around Saint-Nom-de-Jésus, has
the fewest children and the fewest immigrants of the five, the most French at home, and the
most residents who moved in the last five years, which reads as a young, mobile, francophone
population. Pointe-Saint-Charles around Charles-Lemoyne is polarised: household income is in
the top three deciles and so is the low-income rate, because the circle reaches both the
condo towers along the canal and the social housing of the Pointe. Saint-Germain's zone stands
apart on education far more than on income.
:::

Two composite indices computed by other institutions offer a cross-check (@tbl-indices). The
INSPQ index has a material axis (income, education, employment) and a social axis (people
living alone, lone-parent families, separated or widowed); the table shows the share of each
zone's residents living in areas ranked in the two most deprived quintiles for Quebec. The
city's equity index adds environment, access to services and safety, on the city's own
territory only.

::: {.column-page}

|:---|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

| In socially deprived DAs (INSPQ Q4-5) | % of residents | 80 [d6]{.decile-mid} | 86 [d7]{.decile-mid} | 88 [d8]{.decile-high} | 94 [d9]{.decile-high} | 56 [d3]{.decile-low} | 76 |
| Equity index IEMV 2026 (0 best, 6 worst) | score | 2.4 [d6]{.decile-mid} | 1.9 [d3]{.decile-low} | 1.7 [d2]{.decile-low} | 1.8 [d3]{.decile-low} | 1.3 [d1]{.decile-low} | 2.3 |

: Two composite indices computed by others: INSPQ material and social deprivation (share of residents in the two most deprived quintiles) and the city's 2026 equity index (population-weighted mean, 0 least vulnerable to 6 most) {#tbl-indices}
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Social deprivation is high almost everywhere in central Montreal

Three quarters of residents around the median island school live in areas the INSPQ ranks as
socially deprived. The social axis counts people living alone and lone-parent families, and
the dense central boroughs are full of both. It says something about the household mix, not
about whether a neighbourhood is bad for a child, and it should be read alongside the
households-with-children line of @tbl-people rather than on its own.
:::

# Safety

@tbl-safety combines two datasets. SPVM incidents are counted inside the circle for the last
three complete years and divided by the circle's residents; the SAAQ collision extract counts
pedestrian and cyclist victims within 500 m of the school door, the distance a child walks.

::: {.column-page}

| Break-ins | /1000/yr | 3.3 [d7]{.decile-mid} | 2.9 [d6]{.decile-mid} | 4.4 [d9]{.decile-high} | 7.4 [d10]{.decile-high} | 2.7 [d6]{.decile-mid} | 2.6 |
| Vehicle theft and theft from vehicles | /1000/yr | 6.3 [d7]{.decile-mid} | 5.9 [d6]{.decile-mid} | 7.1 [d9]{.decile-high} | 9.5 [d10]{.decile-high} | 3.5 [d1]{.decile-low} | 5.6 |

| Pedestrian and cyclist victims within 500 m | /yr | 8.8 [d8]{.decile-high} | 3.0 [d4]{.decile-mid} | 4.2 [d5]{.decile-mid} | 12.2 [d9]{.decile-high} | 5.6 [d6]{.decile-mid} | 4.6 |

: Safety: SPVM incidents 2023 to 2025 per 1 000 residents per year within 1 km, and SAAQ pedestrian and cyclist victims 2017 to 2021 within 500 m of the school, per year {#tbl-safety}
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reading the table

The Saint-Nom-de-Jésus circle is in the top decile on every crime category, and its break-in
rate is close to three times the island median. The SPVM file only says where and what, not
why, but the circle covers the commercial strip of rue Ontario and its side streets. The
pedestrian and cyclist line singles out two zones, Saint-Barthélemy and Saint-Nom-de-Jésus,
whose 500 m circles include arterial streets. La Vérendrye and Saint-Germain are the quiet
ones on both counts.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## What these two datasets cannot say

The city states that the incident file is not official SPVM statistics. Positions are moved to
the nearest intersection, so nothing finer than a few hundred metres is meaningful, and 17% of
incidents in the file have no coordinates at all and are absent from every rate above. The
collision extract ends in 2021 on both the city and Données Québec portals, and the last two of
its five years are pandemic years with fewer trips. Both are rates of reported events, not of
risk.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Reading the tables

Villeray and Tétreaultville are the plex belt: more than half of all dwellings are in two- to
five-unit buildings, and Tétreaultville is the cheapest of the five to buy into on every
housing type. Pointe-Saint-Charles is the outlier in stock, almost half condominiums with a
median build year of 1990, because the circle reaches the redeveloped canal frontage. The
Outremont zone is assessed at roughly two and a half times the island median on every type.
The effective tax rate barely moves across the five, so the tax bill is the assessed value
in disguise: the borough taxes on the last two lines of the account shown earlier are small
next to the general tax.
:::

| Park area per 1 000 residents | ha | 0.24 [d1]{.decile-low} | 1.45 [d7]{.decile-mid} | 1.12 [d6]{.decile-mid} | 1.00 [d6]{.decile-mid} | 2.02 [d9]{.decile-high} | 0.96 |

: Parks within 1 km (large parks and borough parks only) {#tbl-parks}
:::

The Saint-Barthélemy circle is in the bottom decile on both park lines: the most populous of
the five zones has the least park space, in area and per resident. The circle holds only small
borough parks, the largest under three hectares; the nearest large park, Parc Jarry, is about
two kilometres west of the school. Whether that counts as the school's neighbourhood is exactly
the kind of question a fixed circle cannot answer and a real catchment polygon would settle.

# Quirks found along the way

::: {.callout-note}
## Five things the scripts had to absorb

1. **The city's portal refuses plain downloads.** Requests without a browser-like User-Agent
   get a 19-byte `RBAC: access denied` body with a 200 status. The fetcher sends a User-Agent
   and rejects any tiny download that starts that way.
2. **Non-residential tax lines are tiered.** A non-residential account carries its value split
   across a "≤ 900 000" and a "> 900 000" line, so the value on the general-tax line is capped.
   The collapse step takes the line value for residential classes only.
3. **No 2016 population at dissemination-area level.** Boundaries changed between censuses, so
   the "population change" metric planned in the brief is not computable and was dropped.
4. **Pandas drops all-empty columns when pivoting.** The census extract silently lost the
   2016 column before it was noticed; the extractor now reindexes to the full variable list.
5. **The collision extract is older than advertised.** Both the city and Données Québec copies
   end in 2021; the newer SAAQ years are not on either portal.
:::

# Conclusion

Across five zones and 229 reference schools, the open data:

- **Separates two zones in the same borough.** Tétreaultville and Hochelaga share a borough and
  differ by two to four deciles on children, mobility, crime and housing type (@tbl-people,
  @tbl-safety, @tbl-stock).
- **Replaces the commercial price and tax sites.** The tax-bill file gives a per-unit assessed
  value and bill by housing type for 99.7% of accounts, and shows that the effective tax rate
  varies little between boroughs (@tbl-cost).
- **Puts a number on things a borough average hides**, such as the bottom-decile park share
  around Saint-Barthélemy (@tbl-parks) and the polarised income profile around Charles-Lemoyne
  (@tbl-people).
- **Runs fast enough to be interactive.** Once the data is cached, all 229 zones compute in
  under ten seconds.

Next steps, in order:

1. **Real zone polygons.** Digitise or obtain the catchments from the three service centres'
   finders, then replace the circle. Every metric above is written to take any polygon.
2. **Childcare, transit and heat.** The Ministère de la Famille daycare list (places per child
   under five, needs geocoding), STM morning departures, and the INSPQ heat-island raster are
   the next three sources the brief ranks highest.
3. **The secondary school each zone feeds.** A hand-built lookup from the service centres'
   board resolutions; the single most useful fact this post cannot yet give.
4. **A map of all 229 zones** for each metric, so a parent can start from the map rather than
   from a school name.

::: {.callout-important}
## Bottom line

Once the school is chosen, the kilometre around it can be described in thirty-four sourced,
comparable numbers from open data in a few seconds, without a single scrape of a broker site.
What the numbers cannot yet do is follow the real zone boundary, and that is the next thing to
build.
:::
